chunks.text: Yosemite National Park is located in the Sierra Nevada mountains of California. It was established as a national park on October 1, 1890. The park covers approximately 748,436 acres (1,169 square miles) and is visited by over 4 million people each year. Yosemite is internationally recognized for its granite cliffs, waterfalls, clear streams, giant sequoia groves, lakes, mountains, meadows, glaciers, and biological diversity. Almost 95 percent of the park is designated wilderness. Yosemite Valley, only 7 miles long, is the centerpiece of the park. The park ranges in elevation from 2,127 feet to 13,114 feet at Mount Lyell, the highest point in the park.

El Capitan is a vertical rock formation in Yosemite National Park. At approximately 3,000 feet (900 meters) from base to summit on its tallest face, it is one of the world's largest granite monoliths. El Capitan is located at the north side of Yosemite Valley, near its western end. The granite that forms El Capitan is approximately 100 million years old. It is a popular destination for rock climbers worldwide. The first free ascent of The Nose route was completed by Lynn Hill in 1993. The Dawn Wall, considered one of the most difficult big wall climbs in the world, was first free-climbed by Tommy Caldwell and Kevin Jorgeson in January 2015. Climbers typically take several days to ascend El Capitan, sleeping in portaledges attached to the rock face.

Half Dome is a granite dome at the eastern end of Yosemite Valley. It rises more than 4,737 feet (1,444 meters) above the valley floor and 8,844 feet (2,695 meters) above sea level. Half Dome is Yosemite's most iconic feature. A permit is required to hike to the top of Half Dome. Permits are available through a preseason lottery (March) and a daily lottery two days before each hiking date. The hike to the summit is approximately 14 to 16 miles round trip and takes 10 to 12 hours. The final 400 feet of the ascent is along a steep cable route that is only available when cables are up, typically from late May through mid-October, weather permitting. The cables are taken down in winter. Only 300 hikers per day are allowed on the cables. Hikers should start very early in the morning and must carry adequate water, food, and rain gear.

Yosemite Falls is the highest waterfall in Yosemite National Park and one of the tallest in North America. It drops a total of 2,425 feet (739 meters) from the top of the upper fall to the base of the lower fall. Yosemite Falls is composed of three sections: Upper Yosemite Fall (1,430 feet), the middle cascades (675 feet), and Lower Yosemite Fall (320 feet). The falls are at their peak flow in May and June during spring snowmelt. By August, the falls often slow to a trickle or dry up completely. The Lower Yosemite Fall trail is a short, easy 1-mile loop that is wheelchair accessible. The Upper Yosemite Fall trail is a strenuous 7.2-mile round trip hike with 2,700 feet of elevation gain.

Black bears are common in Yosemite National Park. There are estimated to be 300 to 500 black bears in the park. Despite their name, black bears in Yosemite can be black, brown, cinnamon, or blonde in color. Bears in Yosemite are wild animals and can be dangerous. Visitors must store all food, coolers, and anything with a scent (including toiletries, sunscreen, and trash) in bear-proof food lockers provided at all campgrounds and trailheads, or in bear canisters while in the backcountry. Bear canisters are required for all overnight trips in Yosemite's wilderness. Approved bear canisters can be rented at the Yosemite Valley Wilderness Center, Tuolumne Meadows Wilderness Center, Big Oak Flat Information Station, and Wawona Visitor Center. If you encounter a bear, do not run. Make noise, appear as large as possible, and throw small rocks or sticks near (not at) the bear to scare it away. Never approach or feed a bear. Feeding bears is illegal and can result in a fine of up to $5,000. Report all bear sightings to the nearest ranger station or call 209-372-0322.

Yosemite has 13 campgrounds with over 1,400 campsites. Reservations are required for most campgrounds and can be made at recreation.gov up to 5 months in advance. The most popular campgrounds include Upper Pines, Lower Pines, and North Pines in Yosemite Valley. Camp 4, a walk-in campground, operates on a first-come, first-served basis and is famous as a climbing camp. Campground fees range from $12 to $36 per night depending on the campground and season. All campgrounds have bear-proof food lockers, picnic tables, and fire rings. Campfires are allowed only in established fire rings and only when fire restrictions are not in effect. Quiet hours are from 10 PM to 6 AM. Maximum stay is 7 days in Yosemite Valley campgrounds (May through September) and 30 days outside the Valley. Pets are allowed in campgrounds but must be on a leash no longer than 6 feet at all times and are not permitted on trails, in wilderness areas, or in public buildings.

Yosemite experiences a Mediterranean climate with warm, dry summers and cool, wet winters. Summer temperatures in Yosemite Valley average 80-100°F (27-38°C) during the day and 50-60°F (10-16°C) at night. Winter temperatures range from 25-55°F (-4 to 13°C). Higher elevations are significantly cooler year-round. Snowfall occurs from November through March, with the park receiving an average of 180 inches of snow at higher elevations. Tioga Road (Highway 120 through the park) and Glacier Point Road typically close from November through late May or June due to snow. Yosemite Valley is accessible year-round via Highway 140 (El Portal Road). Spring (April-June) is the best time to see waterfalls at peak flow. Summer (July-September) is the busiest season with warm weather ideal for hiking. Fall (October-November) offers smaller crowds and changing foliage. Winter (December-March) provides opportunities for snowshoeing, skiing, and viewing the park in snow.

A wilderness permit is required for all overnight trips in Yosemite's wilderness. Permits help protect the wilderness by limiting the number of people in each area. Sixty percent of permits are available by reservation, and 40 percent are available on a first-come, first-served basis starting at 11 AM the day before the trip. Reservations can be made at recreation.gov starting 24 weeks (168 days) before the trip start date. There is a $5 per person reservation fee plus $5 per reservation. Popular trailheads like Happy Isles (for Half Dome/John Muir Trail), Cathedral Lakes, and Clouds Rest fill up quickly—often within minutes of becoming available. Permit holders must watch a Leave No Trace video and pick up their permit at a wilderness center. Backpackers must use approved bear canisters for food storage in the wilderness. Group size is limited to 15 people for day use and 8 people for overnight trips in the wilderness.

In case of emergency in Yosemite, call 911 or contact the nearest ranger station. Cell phone service is limited and unreliable throughout most of the park. There is limited cell coverage in Yosemite Village, Curry Village, and along parts of Tioga Road. The Yosemite Medical Clinic is located in Yosemite Village and is open daily during summer and on weekdays during winter for non-emergency medical care. For search and rescue, Yosemite has a dedicated team that responds to climbing accidents, lost hikers, and other emergencies. If someone is injured on a trail, send another person for help while someone stays with the injured person. Mark the location clearly. For river safety: never swim above waterfalls or in swift water. Over 25 people have died from being swept over waterfalls in Yosemite. Drowning is the number one cause of accidental death in the park. Hantavirus is present in the park—avoid contact with rodents and their droppings, especially in enclosed structures. Lightning is a danger at higher elevations—if thunderstorms approach, descend immediately from ridges, peaks, and exposed areas.

The Yosemite Firefall is a natural phenomenon that occurs in mid-to-late February when conditions are just right. When the setting sun hits Horsetail Fall on El Capitan at a specific angle, the waterfall appears to glow orange and red, resembling a flow of lava or fire. The natural Firefall typically occurs during a two-week window in February, usually around February 15-28. For the phenomenon to be visible, several conditions must align: Horsetail Fall must be flowing (requiring sufficient snowmelt), the sky must be clear at sunset, and the viewer must be positioned correctly. The best viewing spots are along Northside Drive near El Capitan Picnic Area. The park implements traffic management during this period. A historical Firefall, where burning embers were pushed off Glacier Point, was a man-made spectacle that occurred from the 1870s until 1968 when the National Park Service discontinued it.

Yosemite is home to three groves of giant sequoias: the Mariposa Grove (the largest, with about 500 mature trees), the Tuolumne Grove, and the Merced Grove. Giant sequoias are the largest trees on Earth by volume. The Grizzly Giant in Mariposa Grove is estimated to be about 1,800 years old, stands 209 feet tall, and has a circumference of 96 feet at its base. The California Tunnel Tree in Mariposa Grove was tunneled in 1895 and visitors can still walk through it. Giant sequoias depend on fire for reproduction—fire clears the forest floor, creates mineral-rich soil, and the heat opens sequoia cones to release seeds. The bark of giant sequoias can be up to 3 feet thick, providing natural fire resistance. The Mariposa Grove is accessible via a shuttle bus from the Mariposa Grove Welcome Plaza. The Big Trees Loop Trail in Mariposa Grove is a 0.3-mile accessible trail. The Grizzly Giant Loop Trail is a 2-mile moderate hike.

Rock falls are a natural geological process in Yosemite and pose a significant hazard to visitors. An average of 60 to 80 rock falls occur each year in Yosemite Valley. Rock falls can happen at any time and without warning, though they are more common in spring when water seeps into cracks and freezes. Some notable rock falls include the 1996 Happy Isles rock fall that killed one person and injured several others, and the 2017 El Capitan rock fall that killed one climber and injured another. Visitors should avoid lingering at the base of cliffs, especially during and after rain or freeze-thaw cycles. If you hear a rock fall, do not look up—instead, immediately take cover behind a large object or drop to the ground and protect your head. Talus fields (piles of fallen rock at the base of cliffs) indicate areas of frequent rock fall activity and should be traversed quickly.

Yosemite National Park is located approximately 170 miles east of San Francisco and 300 miles north of Los Angeles. The park has four highway entrances: Highway 120 West (Big Oak Flat Road) from the San Francisco Bay Area, Highway 140 (El Portal Road) from Merced, Highway 41 from Fresno, and Highway 120 East (Tioga Pass Road) from the east side of the Sierra. The park entrance fee is $35 per vehicle (valid for 7 days), $30 per motorcycle, or $20 per person for those entering on foot or bicycle. An annual park pass costs $70. Free shuttle buses operate in Yosemite Valley year-round, connecting major lodges, campgrounds, trailheads, and visitor services. The YARTS bus system provides public transit from Merced, Mariposa, and other gateway communities. Parking in Yosemite Valley is extremely limited during summer months—visitors are encouraged to use shuttles or arrive early.
